  --event EVENTS
    • Replace ALIAS with the alias of an HyperVault Server.
    • Replace BUCKET with the name of the bucket in which to configure the event.
    • Replace EVENTS with a comma-separated list of events for which HyperVault triggers notifications.

    Use mc event ls to view all configured bucket events for a given notification target:

    mc event ls ALIAS/BUCKET arn:hypervault:sqs::primary:webhook

  4. Validate the configured events.

    Perform an action on the bucket for which you configured the new event and check the webhook service for the notification data. The action required depends on which events were specified when configuring the bucket notification.

    For example, if the bucket notification configuration includes the s3:ObjectCreated:Put event, you can use the mc cp command to create a new object in the bucket and trigger a notification.

    mc cp ~/data/new-object.txt ALIAS/BUCKET

Update a webhook endpoint in an HyperVault Server

The following procedure updates an existing webhook service endpoint for supporting bucket notifications in an HyperVault Server.

  1. List configured webhook endpoints in the deployment.

    Use the mc admin config get command to list the currently configured webhook service endpoints in the deployment:

    mc admin config get ALIAS notify_webhook

    Replace ALIAS with the alias of the HyperVault Server.

    The command output resembles the following:

    notify_webhook:primary endpoint="https://webhook.example.com" auth_token="" queue_limit="0" queue_dir="" client_cert="" client_key=""
notify_webhook:secondary endpoint="https://webhook.example.com" auth_token="" queue_limit="0" queue_dir="" client_cert="" client_key=""
    • notify_webhook is the top-level configuration key for a Webhook Service Notification Settings.
    • endpoint specifies the webhook service endpoint for the given notify_webhook key.
    • The notify_webhook:<IDENTIFIER> suffix describes the unique identifier for that webhook service endpoint.

    Note the identifier for the webhook service endpoint you want to update for the next step.

  2. Update the webhook endpoint.

    Use the mc admin config set command to set the new configuration for the webhook service endpoint:

    mc admin config set ALIAS notify_webhook:IDENTIFIER \
   endpoint="<ENDPOINT>" \
   auth_token="<string>" \
   queue_dir="<string>" \
   queue_limit="<string>" \
   client_cert="<string>" \
   client_key="<string>" \
   comment="<string>"
    • The notify_webhook endpoint configuration setting is the minimum required for a webhook service endpoint.
    • All other configuration settings are optional.

    See Webhook Service Notification Settings for a complete list of webhook configuration settings.

  3. Restart the HyperVault Server.

    You must restart the HyperVault Server to apply the configuration changes. Use the mc admin service restart command to restart the deployment.

    mc admin service restart ALIAS

    Replace ALIAS with the alias of the deployment to restart.

    The hypervault server process prints a line on startup for each configured webhook target similar to the following:

    SQS ARNs: arn:hypervault:sqs::primary:webhook

  4. Validate the changes.

    Perform an action on a bucket which has an event configuration using the updated webhook service endpoint and check the webhook service for the notification data. The action required depends on which events were specified when configuring the bucket notification.

    For example, if the bucket notification configuration includes the s3:ObjectCreated:Put event, you can use the mc cp command to create a new object in the bucket and trigger a notification.

    mc cp ~/data/new-object.txt ALIAS/BUCKET

title: Bucket Quotas | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Bucket Quotas

Best-effort enforcement
Bucket quota enforcement is best-effort and not real-time. HyperVault evaluates quota usage periodically through its internal scanner, so a bucket may temporarily exceed its configured quota between scanner cycles. Bucket hard-quota enforcement is wired only into the S3 API request handlers, Internal processes like Inventory will not go through quota enforcement. Do not rely on bucket quotas as a hard ceiling for safety-critical storage limits.

HyperVault supports setting hard quotas on buckets to limit the total amount of data a bucket can store. When a bucket reaches its configured quota, HyperVault rejects further write operations to that bucket until data is removed to bring usage below the limit.

Bucket quotas are not available when HyperVault runs in S3 Express One Zone mode.

Set a hard quota

Use mc quota set to set a hard quota on a bucket. The --size flag specifies the maximum storage size for the bucket.

mc quota set ALIAS/BUCKET --size SIZE

Replace SIZE with a value and unit suffix, for example 1GB, 10GB, or 500MB.

The following example sets a 1 GB hard quota on the mybucket bucket:

mc quota set myhypervault/mybucket --size 1GB

When the total size of objects in the bucket reaches the quota, HyperVault returns an error for any further PUT operations.

Verify the quota

To view the current quota configuration for a bucket:

mc quota info ALIAS/BUCKET

Clear a quota

To remove the quota from a bucket:

mc quota clear ALIAS/BUCKET

Required permissions

The user or service account performing quota operations must have the following admin permissions:

Permission Description
admin:SetBucketQuota Allows setting or clearing a bucket quota.
admin:GetBucketQuota Allows retrieving the current bucket quota.

The built-in consoleAdmin policy includes both of these permissions.

Monitoring

HyperVault exposes bucket quota metrics for integration with Prometheus or other monitoring systems:

  • v3 metric: hypervault_cluster_usage_buckets_quota_total_bytes (labels: bucket)
  • v2 metric: hypervault_bucket_quota_total_bytes (labels: bucket, server)

See Metrics and Alerts for more information on configuring monitoring.

title: Identity and Access Management | HyperVault DocumentationHow HyperVault authorizes a request
html:
Identity and Access Management

HyperVault requires authentication and authorization for every operation on the object store. Human users and client applications must authenticate, and can perform only operations on resources explicitly allowed by the access policies assigned to them.

Authentication verifies the identity of a user or client application. User credentials take the form of a username and password. Application credentials can take the form of an access key and secret key, or an application can call the appropriate STS endpoint. Which endpoint depends on your identity provider.

Authorization defines the actions an authenticated user or application can perform, and the resources they can access. HyperVault implements policy-based access control (PBAC), in which a policy consists of one or more rules that define specific access permissions. By default, HyperVault denies access to any action or resource that is not explicitly granted by an assigned policy. A user with no explicitly assigned or inherited policies cannot perform any S3 or HyperVault administrative API operations.

Identity management

HyperVault supports multiple identity providers for authenticating users and applications:

Provider Description
Built-in Manage users and groups directly within HyperVault
OpenID Connect Integrate with OIDC providers (Okta, Auth0, Keycloak, Google)
Active Directory/LDAP Authenticate against directory services
X.509 certificate Authenticate with a client certificate or SPIFFE SVID
Kubernetes service account Authenticate in-cluster workloads with their service account token
Authentication plugin Implement custom authentication logic

See Identity Management for details on configuring multiple providers.

Human users are typically identified with a username and password, regardless of the identity provider.

Limited access for applications

For application access only, you can create access keys (formerly known as service accounts). An access key is a child identity of a HyperVault user, and inherits its access rights from the policies assigned to its parent user. You can also assign an additional inline policy to an access key account to further restrict access.

You can create access keys with mc or the console even if you manage your users with an external identity provider.

For short-lived application access, you can call the endpoint of the Security Token Service (STS) API that your identity provider supports. For more information, see individual pages for configuring identity providers, and the STS reference documentation.

Root user

The HyperVault root user has access to all actions and resources on the deployment. This user is created when the deployment first starts. You set the username and password for the root user with environment variables (default value for each hypervaultadmin):

  • HYPERVAULT_ROOT_USER
  • HYPERVAULT_ROOT_PASSWORD

Consider implementing the following best practices for managing your root user account:

  • Specify long, unique, and random strings for root credentials.

  • Make sure that only known and trusted individuals who require superuser access can retrieve these credentials.

  • Do not use these credentials for regular client access, whether the environment is production or not

Access management

HyperVault implements Policy-Based Access Control (PBAC) to define the authorized actions and resources to which an authenticated user or application has access. Each policy describes one or more actions and conditions that outline the permissions of a user or group of users.

Depending on your choice of identity provider, you can assign policies to individual users or to groups of users.

If you work with the built-in identity manager or with Active Directory/LDAP, you can assign policies to users or to groups. If you work with an OIDC provider, you can assign policies through the provider’s role_policy setting or through a user’s policy claim.

HyperVault PBAC is built for compatibility with AWS IAM policy syntax, structure, and behavior. For details, see Access Control with Policy Management. This documentation covers HyperVault IAM, but see also the AWS documentation for IAM.

Deny Overrides Allow

HyperVault follows AWS IAM policy evaluation rules. HyperVault evaluates every Deny rule before any Allow rule. A Deny rule overrides an Allow rule when the request matches that rule’s action, resource, and conditions. For example, a user has a policy with an Allow rule for a resource, and a group the user belongs to has a policy with a Deny rule for that same resource. HyperVault applies the Deny rule.

For more information, see the AWS documentation on Policy evaluation logic.

title: Access Control with Policy Management | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Access Control with Policy Management

HyperVault uses Policy-Based Access Control (PBAC) to define the authorized actions and resources to which an authenticated user has access. Each policy describes one or more actions and conditions that outline the permissions of a user or group of users.

HyperVault PBAC is built for compatibility with AWS IAM policy syntax, structure, and behavior. This documentation makes a best-effort to cover IAM-specific behavior and functionality. Refer also to the AWS IAM documentation for more information.

The mc admin policy command supports creation and management of policies on the HyperVault deployment. See the command reference for examples of usage.

How a policy reaches an authenticated user depends on the identity provider that authenticated them:

  • With Active Directory or LDAP, HyperVault matches policies by name against the user distinguished name and any group distinguished names.
  • With OpenID Connect, the policy comes from the RoleArn used for the request, or from a claim inside the token.

You can also hand authorization to an external service instead of evaluating policies here. The authorization plugin answers ALLOW or DENY for every authenticated API call.

Built-in policies

HyperVault provides the following built-in policies for assigning to users or groups.

Policy Grants
consoleAdmin Every administrative, KMS, S3, and S3 Tables action
readwrite Every S3 action on all buckets and objects
readonly Reading a specific object, without listing
consolereadonly Reading objects, plus listing so the Console can browse
writeonly Writing a specific object, without listing
diagnostics Diagnostic and profiling actions
iamAdmin Managing users, groups, policies, and accounts, with no data access
infraAdmin Cluster, service, and capacity administration, with no IAM or data access
replicationAdmin Site, bucket, and table replication administration
securityAuditAdmin Read-only visibility into identities, configuration, and cluster state
tablesAdmin Every HyperVault Tables action
tablesReadWrite Reading and writing HyperVault Tables data and metadata
tablesReadOnly Reading HyperVault Tables data and metadata

Run mc admin policy info against a deployment to print the exact document for any of these policies.

consoleAdmin

Grants complete access to all S3 and administrative API operations against all resources on the HyperVault deployment. Equivalent to the following set of actions:

  • s3:*

  • admin:*

  • kms:*

  • s3tables:*

readonly

Grants read-only permissions on any object on the HyperVault deployment. The GET action must apply to a specific object without requiring any listing. Equivalent to the following set of actions:

  • s3:GetBucketLocation

  • s3:GetObject

The policy also explicitly denies admin:CreateUser.

This policy supports GET operations on objects at a specific path, such as GET play/mybucket/object.file. The following commands use those operations:

  • mc cp

  • mc stat

  • mc head

  • mc cat

The exclusion of listing permissions is intentional, as typical use cases do not intend for a “read-only” role to have complete discoverability (listing all buckets and objects) on the object storage resource.

consolereadonly

Grants the same read access as readonly, and adds s3:ListBucket so that the Console UI can browse buckets. Equivalent to the following set of actions:

  • s3:GetBucketLocation

  • s3:GetObject

  • s3:ListBucket

The policy also explicitly denies admin:CreateUser.

readwrite

Grants read and write permissions for all buckets and objects on the HyperVault server. Equivalent to s3:*.

diagnostics

Grants permission to perform diagnostic actions on the HyperVault deployment. Includes the following actions:

  • admin:ServerTrace

  • admin:Profiling

  • admin:ConsoleLog

  • admin:ServerInfo

  • admin:TopLocksInfo

  • admin:OBDInfo

  • admin:BandwidthMonitor

  • admin:Prometheus

writeonly

Grants write-only permissions to any namespace in the HyperVault deployment (bucket and path to object). The PUT action must apply to a specific object location without requiring any listing. Equivalent to the s3:PutObject action.

iamAdmin

Grants identity and access management without any infrastructure, diagnostic, or S3 data access. Use it to delegate user and policy administration without granting access to stored objects. Includes the following actions:

  • admin:CreateUser, admin:DeleteUser, admin:ListUsers, admin:EnableUser, admin:DisableUser, admin:GetUser
  • admin:AddUserToGroup, admin:RemoveUserFromGroup, admin:GetGroup, admin:ListGroups, admin:EnableGroup, admin:DisableGroup
  • admin:CreatePolicy, admin:DeletePolicy, admin:GetPolicy, admin:AttachUserOrGroupPolicy, admin:UpdatePolicyAssociation, admin:ListUserPolicies
  • admin:CreateServiceAccount, admin:UpdateServiceAccount, admin:RemoveServiceAccount, admin:ListServiceAccounts, admin:ListTemporaryAccounts
  • admin:ExportIAM, admin:ImportIAM

infraAdmin

Grants cluster and service administration without any IAM or S3 data access. Includes the following actions:

  • admin:ServerUpdate, admin:ServiceRestart, admin:ServiceStop, admin:ServiceFreeze, admin:ServiceCordon
  • admin:ServerInfo, admin:StorageInfo, admin:ConfigUpdate, admin:Heal, admin:ForceUnlock
  • admin:Decommission, admin:Rebalance, admin:SetBucketQuota, admin:GetBucketQuota, admin:SetTier, admin:ListTier
  • admin:LicenseInfo, admin:DataUsageInfo, admin:ImportBucketMetadata, admin:ExportBucketMetadata
  • admin:StartBatchJob, admin:ListBatchJobs, admin:DescribeBatchJob, admin:CancelBatchJob, admin:GenerateBatchJob, admin:InventoryControl
  • admin:ClusterInfo, admin:PoolList, admin:PoolInfo, admin:NodeList, admin:NodeInfo, admin:SetInfo, admin:DriveList, admin:DriveInfo

replicationAdmin

Grants administration of site, bucket, and table replication. Includes the following administrative actions:

  • admin:SiteReplicationAdd, admin:SiteReplicationDisable, admin:SiteReplicationRemove, admin:SiteReplicationResync, admin:SiteReplicationInfo, admin:SiteReplicationOperation
  • admin:TablesReplicationAdd, admin:TablesReplicationRemove, admin:TablesReplicationInfo, admin:TablesReplicationStartFailover, admin:TablesReplicationCatalogAdmin
  • admin:ReplicationDiff

It also includes the following S3 actions on all resources:

  • s3:GetReplicationConfiguration, s3:PutReplicationConfiguration, s3:ResetBucketReplicationState, s3:GetObjectVersionForReplication

securityAuditAdmin

Grants read-only visibility into identities, bucket configuration, and cluster state, with no ability to change them and no access to object data. Includes the following administrative actions:

  • admin:ListUsers, admin:GetUser, admin:ListGroups, admin:GetGroup, admin:GetPolicy, admin:ListUserPolicies
  • admin:ListServiceAccounts, admin:ListTemporaryAccounts, admin:ExportIAM
  • admin:SiteReplicationInfo, admin:TablesReplicationInfo

Each user can access only the resources and operations which are explicitly assigned to the built-in role. HyperVault denies access to any other resource or action.

Deny Overrides Allow

HyperVault follows AWS IAM policy evaluation rules. HyperVault evaluates every Deny rule before any Allow rule. A Deny rule overrides an Allow rule when the request matches that rule’s action, resource, and conditions. For example, a user has a policy with an Allow rule for a resource, and a group the user belongs to has a policy with a Deny rule for that same resource. HyperVault applies the Deny rule.

For more information, see the AWS documentation on Policy evaluation logic.

Policy document structure

HyperVault policy documents use the same schema as AWS IAM Policy documents.

The following sample document provides a template for creating custom policies for use with a HyperVault deployment. For more complete documentation on IAM policy elements, see the IAM JSON Policy Elements Reference.

The maximum size for any single policy document is 20KiB. There is no limit to the number of policy documents that can be attached to a user or group.

{
      "Version" : "2012-10-17",
      "Statement" : [
            { "Effect" : "Allow",
              "Action" : [ "s3:<ActionName>", ... ],
              "Resource" : "arn:aws:s3:::*",
              "Condition" : { ... }
            },
            { "Effect" : "Deny",
              "Action" : [ "s3:<ActionName>", ... ],
              "Resource" : "arn:aws:s3:::*",
              "Condition" : { ... }
            }
      ]
}

  • For the Statement.Action array, specify one or more supported S3 API operations.

  • For the Statement.Resource key, specify the bucket or bucket prefix to which to restrict the policy. You can use * and ? wildcard characters as per the S3 Resource Spec.

    The * wildcard may result in unintended application of a policy to multiple buckets or prefixes based on the pattern match. For example, arn:aws:s3:::data* would match the buckets data, data_private, and data_internal. Specifying only * as the resource key applies the policy to all buckets and prefixes on the deployment.

  • For the Statement.Condition key, you can specify one or more supported Conditions.

Supported S3 Policy Condition Keys

HyperVault policy documents support IAM conditional statements.

Each condition element consists of operators and condition keys. HyperVault supports a subset of IAM condition keys. For complete information on any listed condition key, see the IAM Condition Element Documentation

HyperVault supports the following condition keys for all supported actions:

  • aws:Referer

  • aws:SourceIp

  • aws:UserAgent

  • aws:SecureTransport

  • aws:CurrentTime

  • aws:EpochTime

  • aws:PrincipalType

  • aws:userid

  • aws:username

  • aws:groups

  • x-amz-content-sha256

  • s3:signatureAge

Warning

The aws:Referer, aws:SourceIp, and aws.UserAgent keys may be easily spoofed and therefore pose a potential security risk. HyperVault recommends using these condition keys only to deny access as a secondary security measure.

Never use these three keys to grant access by themselves.

For aws:SourceIp, use the api trusted_upstream_proxies setting (HYPERVAULT_API_TRUSTED_UPSTREAM_PROXIES) to control which upstream proxies may set the source IP through a forwarded header. The default trusts all proxies, which allows callers to spoof their source IP through forged forwarded headers.

For additional keys supported by a specific S3 action, see the reference documentation for that action.

HyperVault Extended Condition Keys

HyperVault extends the S3 standard condition keys with the following extended key:

sts:DurationSeconds

Specify a time in seconds to limit the duration of all Security Token Service credentials generated by AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity.

This value overrides the DurationSeconds field specified to the client.

For example:

{
      "Version": "2012-10-17",
      "Statement": [
      {
            "Effect": "Deny",
            "Action": [
                  "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity"
            ],
            "Condition": {
                  "NumericGreaterThanEquals": {
                  "sts:DurationSeconds": "300"
                  }
            }
      }
   ]
}

Policy variables

HyperVault supports using policy variables for automatically substituting context from the authenticated user and/or the operation into the user’s assigned policy or policies. Use the ${POLICYVARIABLE} format to specify the variable to the policy as part of the Condition or Resource definition. HyperVault policy variables function similarly to AWS IAM policy elements: Variables and tags.

Each HyperVault identity provider supports its own set of policy variables:

  • HyperVault Policy Variables

  • OpenID Policy Variables

  • Active Directory / LDAP Policy Variables

HyperVault policy variables

The following table contains a list of recommended policy variables for use in authorizing HyperVault-managed users:

Variable Description
aws:referrer The referrer in the HTTP header for the authenticated API call.
aws:SourceIp The source IP in the HTTP header for the authenticated API call.
aws:username The name of the user associated with the authenticated API call.
aws:groups An array of the group names mapped to the authenticated user. For OpenID this maps to the jwt:groups claim; for AD/LDAP this maps to ldap:groups (the group Distinguished Names). Because it is multi-valued, use it with set-style condition operators, for example StringEquals with a list.

For example, the following policy uses variables to substitute the authenticated user’s username as part of the Resource field such that the user can access only the prefixes that match their username:

{
      "Version": "2012-10-17",
      "Statement": [
            {
            "Action": ["s3:ListBucket"],
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::mybucket"],
            "Condition": {"StringLike": {"s3:prefix": ["${aws:username}/**"]}}
            },
            {
            "Action": [
            "s3:GetObject",
            "s3:PutObject"
            ],
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::mybucket/${aws:username}/**"]
            }
      ]
}

HyperVault replaces the ${aws:username} variable in the Resource field with the username. HyperVault then evaluates the policy and allows or denies access to the requested resource and action.

jwt:phone_number Returns the phone_number claim for the user.
jwt:address Returns the address claim for the user.
jwt:scope Returns the scope claim for the user.
jwt:client_id Returns the client_id claim for the user.

See the OpenID Connect Core 1.0 specification for more information on these scopes. Your OIDC provider of choice may have more specific documentation.

For example, the following policy uses variables to substitute the authenticated user’s preferred_username as part of the Resource field such that the user can only access those prefixes which match their username:

{
      "Version": "2012-10-17",
      "Statement": [
            {
                  "Action": ["s3:ListBucket"],
                  "Effect": "Allow",
                  "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::mybucket"],
                  "Condition": {"StringLike": {"s3:prefix": ["${jwt:preferred_username}/*"]}}
            },
            {
                  "Action": [
                        "s3:GetObject",
                        "s3:PutObject"
                  ],
                  "Effect": "Allow",
                  "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::mybucket/${jwt:preferred_username}/*"]
            }
      ]
}

HyperVault replaces the ${jwt:preferred_username} variable in the Resource field with the value of the preferred_username in the JWT token. HyperVault then evaluates the policy and grants or revokes access to the requested API and resource.

Active Directory / LDAP policy variables

The following table contains a list of supported policy variables for use in authorizing AD/LDAP users:

Variable Description
ldap:username The simple username (name) for the authenticated user.
This is distinct from the user’s DistinguishedName or CommonName.
ldap:user The Distinguished Name used by the authenticated user.
ldap:groups The Group Distinguished Name for the authenticated user.

For example, the following policy uses variables to substitute the authenticated user’s name as part of the Resource field such that the user can only access those prefixes which match their name:

{
      "Version": "2012-10-17",
      "Statement": [
            {
                  "Action": ["s3:ListBucket"],
                  "Effect": "Allow",
                  "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::mybucket"],
                  "Condition": {"StringLike": {"s3:prefix": ["${ldap:username}/*"]}}
            },
            {
                  "Action": [
                  "s3:GetObject",
                  "s3:PutObject"
                  ],
                  "Effect": "Allow",
                  "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::mybucket/${ldap:username}/*"]
            }
      ]
}

HyperVault replaces the ${ldap:username} variable in the Resource field with the value of the authenticated user’s name. HyperVault then evaluates the policy and grants or revokes access to the requested API and resource.
text: Access Control with Policy Management MinIO AIStor uses Policy-Based Access Control (PBAC) to define the authorized actions and resources to which an authenticated user has access. Each policy describes one or more actions and conditions that outline the permissions of a user or group of users. MinIO AIStor PBAC is built for compatibility with AWS IAM policy syntax, structure, and behavior. This documentation makes a best-effort to cover IAM-specific behavior and functionality. Refer also to the AWS IAM documentation for more information. The mc admin policy command supports creation and management of policies on the MinIO AIStor deployment. See the command reference for examples of usage. How a policy reaches an authenticated user depends on the identity provider that authenticated them: With Active Directory or LDAP, AIStor matches policies by name against the user distinguished name and any group distinguished names. With OpenID Connect, the policy comes from the RoleArn used for the request, or from a claim inside the token. You can also hand authorization to an external service instead of evaluating policies here. The authorization plugin answers ALLOW or DENY for every authenticated API call. Built-in policies MinIO AIStor provides the following built-in policies for assigning to users or groups. Policy Grants consoleAdmin Every administrative, KMS, S3, and S3 Tables action readwrite Every S3 action on all buckets and objects readonly Reading a specific object, without listing consolereadonly Reading objects, plus listing so the Console can browse writeonly Writing a specific object, without listing diagnostics Diagnostic and profiling actions iamAdmin Managing users, groups, policies, and accounts, with no data access infraAdmin Cluster, service, and capacity administration, with no IAM or data access replicationAdmin Site, bucket, and table replication administration securityAuditAdmin Read-only visibility into identities, configuration, and cluster state tablesAdmin Every AIStor Tables action tablesReadWrite Reading and writing AIStor Tables data and metadata tablesReadOnly Reading AIStor Tables data and metadata Run mc admin policy info against a deployment to print the exact document for any of these policies. consoleAdmin Grants complete access to all S3 and administrative API operations against all resources on the MinIO AIStor deployment. Equivalent to the following set of actions: s3:* admin:* kms:* s3tables:* readonly Grants read-only permissions on any object on the MinIO AIStor deployment. The GET action must apply to a specific object without requiring any listing. Equivalent to the following set of actions: s3:GetBucketLocation s3:GetObject The policy also explicitly denies admin:CreateUser. This policy supports GET operations on objects at a specific path, such as GET play/mybucket/object.file. The following commands use those operations: mc cp mc stat mc head mc cat The exclusion of listing permissions is intentional, as typical use cases do not intend for a “read-only” role to have complete discoverability (listing all buckets and objects) on the object storage resource. consolereadonly Grants the same read access as readonly, and adds s3:ListBucket so that the Console UI can browse buckets. Equivalent to the following set of actions: s3:GetBucketLocation s3:GetObject s3:ListBucket The policy also explicitly denies admin:CreateUser. readwrite Grants read and write permissions for all buckets and objects on the MinIO AIStor server. Equivalent to s3:*. diagnostics Grants permission to perform diagnostic actions on the MinIO AIStor deployment. Includes the following actions: admin:ServerTrace admin:Profiling admin:ConsoleLog admin:ServerInfo admin:TopLocksInfo admin:OBDInfo admin:BandwidthMonitor admin:Prometheus writeonly Grants write-only permissions to any namespace in the MinIO AIStor deployment (bucket and path to object). The PUT action must apply to a specific object location without requiring any listing. Equivalent to the s3:PutObject action. iamAdmin Grants identity and access management without any infrastructure, diagnostic, or S3 data access. Use it to delegate user and policy administration without granting access to stored objects. Includes the following actions: admin:CreateUser, admin:DeleteUser, admin:ListUsers, admin:EnableUser, admin:DisableUser, admin:GetUser admin:AddUserToGroup, admin:RemoveUserFromGroup, admin:GetGroup, admin:ListGroups, admin:EnableGroup, admin:DisableGroup admin:CreatePolicy, admin:DeletePolicy, admin:GetPolicy, admin:AttachUserOrGroupPolicy, admin:UpdatePolicyAssociation, admin:ListUserPolicies admin:CreateServiceAccount, admin:UpdateServiceAccount, admin:RemoveServiceAccount, admin:ListServiceAccounts, admin:ListTemporaryAccounts admin:ExportIAM, admin:ImportIAM infraAdmin Grants cluster and service administration without any IAM or S3 data access. Includes the following actions: admin:ServerUpdate, admin:ServiceRestart, admin:ServiceStop, admin:ServiceFreeze, admin:ServiceCordon admin:ServerInfo, admin:StorageInfo, admin:ConfigUpdate, admin:Heal, admin:ForceUnlock admin:Decommission, admin:Rebalance, admin:SetBucketQuota, admin:GetBucketQuota, admin:SetTier, admin:ListTier admin:LicenseInfo, admin:DataUsageInfo, admin:ImportBucketMetadata, admin:ExportBucketMetadata admin:StartBatchJob, admin:ListBatchJobs, admin:DescribeBatchJob, admin:CancelBatchJob, admin:GenerateBatchJob, admin:InventoryControl admin:ClusterInfo, admin:PoolList, admin:PoolInfo, admin:NodeList, admin:NodeInfo, admin:SetInfo, admin:DriveList, admin:DriveInfo replicationAdmin Grants administration of site, bucket, and table replication. Includes the following administrative actions: admin:SiteReplicationAdd, admin:SiteReplicationDisable, admin:SiteReplicationRemove, admin:SiteReplicationResync, admin:SiteReplicationInfo, admin:SiteReplicationOperation admin:TablesReplicationAdd, admin:TablesReplicationRemove, admin:TablesReplicationInfo, admin:TablesReplicationStartFailover, admin:TablesReplicationCatalogAdmin admin:ReplicationDiff It also includes the following S3 actions on all resources: s3:GetReplicationConfiguration, s3:PutReplicationConfiguration, s3:ResetBucketReplicationState, s3:GetObjectVersionForReplication securityAuditAdmin Grants read-only visibility into identities, bucket configuration, and cluster state, with no ability to change them and no access to object data. Includes the following administrative actions: admin:ListUsers, admin:GetUser, admin:ListGroups, admin:GetGroup, admin:GetPolicy, admin:ListUserPolicies admin:ListServiceAccounts, admin:ListTemporaryAccounts, admin:ExportIAM admin:SiteReplicationInfo, admin:TablesReplicationInfo admin:ServerInfo, admin:StorageInfo, admin:DataUsageInfo, admin:LicenseInfo admin:ClusterInfo, admin:PoolList, admin:PoolInfo, admin:NodeList, admin:NodeInfo, admin:SetInfo, admin:DriveList, admin:DriveInfo admin:Profiling, admin:ServerTrace, admin:ConsoleLog, admin:TopLocksInfo, admin:OBDInfo, admin:BandwidthMonitor, admin:Prometheus It also includes the following S3 actions on all resources: s3:GetBucketPolicy, s3:GetBucketLocation, s3:GetBucketNotification, s3:GetBucketObjectLockConfiguration, s3:GetEncryptionConfiguration, s3:GetBucketTagging, s3:GetBucketVersioning, s3:GetReplicationConfiguration tablesAdmin Grants every AIStor Tables action on all warehouses, namespaces, and tables. Equivalent to s3tables:*. tablesReadWrite Grants read and write access to AIStor Tables data and metadata, without warehouse or policy administration. Includes the following actions: s3tables:GetWarehouse, s3tables:GetWarehouseEncryption, s3tables:GetWarehouseMaintenanceConfiguration, s3tables:GetWarehousePolicy, s3tables:ListWarehouses s3tables:GetNamespace, s3tables:ListNamespaces, s3tables:UpdateNamespaceProperties s3tables:GetTable, s3tables:ListTables, s3tables:GetTableData, s3tables:PutTableData s3tables:GetTableEncryption, s3tables:GetTableMaintenanceConfiguration, s3tables:GetTableMaintenanceJobStatus, s3tables:GetTableMetadataLocation, s3tables:GetTablePolicy s3tables:CreateTable, s3tables:UpdateTable, s3tables:UpdateTableMetadataLocation, s3tables:RenameTable, s3tables:RegisterTable s3tables:GetView, s3tables:ListViews, s3tables:CreateView, s3tables:UpdateView, s3tables:RenameView, s3tables:DeleteView, s3tables:RegisterView s3tables:GetConfig, s3tables:TableMetrics tablesReadOnly Grants read-only access to AIStor Tables data and metadata. Includes the following actions: s3tables:GetWarehouse, s3tables:GetWarehouseEncryption, s3tables:GetWarehouseMaintenanceConfiguration, s3tables:GetWarehousePolicy, s3tables:ListWarehouses s3tables:GetNamespace, s3tables:ListNamespaces s3tables:GetTable, s3tables:ListTables, s3tables:GetTableData s3tables:GetTableEncryption, s3tables:GetTableMaintenanceConfiguration, s3tables:GetTableMaintenanceJobStatus, s3tables:GetTableMetadataLocation, s3tables:GetTablePolicy s3tables:GetView, s3tables:ListViews s3tables:GetConfig, s3tables:TableMetrics Assign default policies Run mc admin policy attach to assign a policy to a user or group. The following table illustrates how you might group users and assign built-in policies on specified resources. User Group Policy Operations Operations readwrite on finance bucketreadonly on audit bucket PUT and GET on finance bucket.GET on audit bucket Auditing readonly on audit bucket GET on audit bucket Admin admin:* All mc admin commands. Each user can access only the resources and operations which are explicitly assigned to the built-in role. MinIO AIStor denies access to any other resource or action. Deny Overrides Allow MinIO AIStor follows AWS IAM policy evaluation rules. MinIO AIStor evaluates every Deny rule before any Allow rule. A Deny rule overrides an Allow rule when the request matches that rule’s action, resource, and conditions. For example, a user has a policy with an Allow rule for a resource, and a group the user belongs to has a policy with a Deny rule for that same resource. MinIO AIStor applies the Deny rule. For more information, see the AWS documentation on Policy evaluation logic. Policy document structure MinIO AIStor policy documents use the same schema as AWS IAM Policy documents. The following sample document provides a template for creating custom policies for use with a MinIO AIStor deployment. For more complete documentation on IAM policy elements, see the IAM JSON Policy Elements Reference. The maximum size for any single policy document is 20KiB. There is no limit to the number of policy documents that can be attached to a user or group. { "Version" : "2012-10-17", "Statement" : [ { "Effect" : "Allow", "Action" : [ "s3:<ActionName>", ... ], "Resource" : "arn:aws:s3:::*", "Condition" : { ... } }, { "Effect" : "Deny", "Action" : [ "s3:<ActionName>", ... ], "Resource" : "arn:aws:s3:::*", "Condition" : { ... } } ] } For the Statement.Action array, specify one or more supported S3 API operations. For the Statement.Resource key, specify the bucket or bucket prefix to which to restrict the policy. You can use * and ? wildcard characters as per the S3 Resource Spec. The * wildcard may result in unintended application of a policy to multiple buckets or prefixes based on the pattern match. For example, arn:aws:s3:::data* would match the buckets data, data_private, and data_internal. Specifying only * as the resource key applies the policy to all buckets and prefixes on the deployment. For the Statement.Condition key, you can specify one or more supported Conditions. Supported S3 policy actions MinIO AIStor policy documents support a subset of IAM S3 Action keys. MinIO AIStor also supports condition keys for some actions beyond the common set of supported keys. Common S3 operations s3:* Selector for all MinIO AIStor S3 operations. Applying this action to a given resource allows the user to perform any S3 operation against that resource. s3:CreateBucket Controls access to the CreateBucket S3 API s3:DeleteBucket Controls access to the DeleteBucket S3 API operation. s3:ForceDeleteBucket Controls access to the DeleteBucket S3 API operation for operations with the x-AIStor-force-delete flag. Required for removing non-empty buckets. s3:GetBucketLocation Controls access to the GetBucketLocation S3 API operation. s3:ListAllMyBuckets Controls access to the ListBuckets s3 API operation. s3:DeleteObject Controls access to the DeleteObject S3 API operation. s3:GetObject Controls access to the GetObject S3 API operation. Supports the following additional condition keys: s3:prefix s3:delimiter s3:max-keys s3:PutObject Controls access to the PutObject S3 API operation. This action is not intended for use with other S3-compatible services. Supported S3 Policy Condition Keys MinIO AIStor policy documents support IAM conditional statements. Each condition element consists of operators and condition keys. MinIO AIStor supports a subset of IAM condition keys. For complete information on any listed condition key, see the IAM Condition Element Documentation MinIO AIStor supports the following condition keys for all supported actions: aws:Referer aws:SourceIp aws:UserAgent aws:SecureTransport aws:CurrentTime aws:EpochTime aws:PrincipalType aws:userid aws:username aws:groups x-amz-content-sha256 s3:signatureAge Warning The aws:Referer, aws:SourceIp, and aws.UserAgent keys may be easily spoofed and therefore pose a potential security risk. MinIO recommends using these condition keys only to deny access as a secondary security measure. Never use these three keys to grant access by themselves. For aws:SourceIp, use the api trusted_upstream_proxies setting (MINIO_API_TRUSTED_UPSTREAM_PROXIES) to control which upstream proxies may set the source IP through a forwarded header. The default trusts all proxies, which allows callers to spoof their source IP through forged forwarded headers. For additional keys supported by a specific S3 action, see the reference documentation for that action. MinIO AIStor Extended Condition Keys MinIO AIStor extends the S3 standard condition keys with the following extended key: sts:DurationSeconds Specify a time in seconds to limit the duration of all Security Token Service credentials generated by AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. This value overrides the DurationSeconds field specified to the client. For example: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Deny", "Action": [ "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity" ], "Condition": { "NumericGreaterThanEquals": { "sts:DurationSeconds": "300" } } } ] } KMS policy action keys MinIO AIStor supports restricting key management service (KMS) actions by policy. You can restrict KMS activities in a policy with any of the following KMS actions: kms:Status Check the status of KMS. kms:Metrics Obtain Prometheus-formatted metrics. kms:API List supported API endpoints. kms:Version Retrieve the KMS version. kms:CreateKey Create a new KMS key. kms:ListKeys Retrieve a list of existing KMS keys. kms:KeyStatus Retrieve the status of a specified KMS key. To select all of the available kms policy actions, use kms:*. KMS actions can be restricted by resource or a resource prefix. The wildcard character * can be used to apply the KMS action policy to all resources that match the prefix. For example, the following policy document allows a user to list keys, create new keys, and check the status of keys for any resource that begins with keys-abc- or myuser-. { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "kms:CreateKey", "kms:KeyStatus", "kms:ListKeys" ], "Resource": [ "arn:minio:kms:::keys-abc-*", "arn:minio:kms:::myuser-*" ] } ] } mc admin Policy Action Keys MinIO AIStor supports the following actions for use with defining policies for mc admin operations. Bucket replication admin:ReplicationDiff Allows computing the set of unreplicated objects in a bucket. Table Sharing access control The following actions control access to Table Sharing operations. Grant these action names individually. MinIO AIStor also accepts the bare admin:DeltaSharing in a policy, but no operation checks it, so a policy that grants only admin:DeltaSharing permits nothing. The policy is accepted without an error, and every share and token operation is denied. admin:DeltaSharingCreateShare Allows creating a new delta share. admin:DeltaSharingUpdateShare Allows modifying an existing delta share configuration. admin:DeltaSharingGetShare Allows viewing an existing delta share configuration. admin:DeltaSharingListShares Allows listing all configured delta shares. admin:DeltaSharingDeleteShare Allows deleting a delta share. admin:DeltaSharingCreateToken Allows creating an access token for an existing delta share. admin:DeltaSharingListTokens Allows listing access tokens created for a delta share. admin:DeltaSharingDeleteToken Allows revoking an active access token for a delta share. mc admin Policy Condition Keys MinIO AIStor supports the following conditions for use with defining policies for mc admin actions. aws:Referer aws:SourceIp aws:UserAgent aws:SecureTransport aws:CurrentTime aws:EpochTime For complete information on any listed condition key, see the IAM Condition Element Documentation. Tag-based policy conditions Policies can use conditions to limit a user’s access only to objects with a specific tag. MinIO AIStor supports tag-based conditionals for policies for selected actions. Use the s3:ExistingObjectTag/<key> in the Condition statement of the policy. Policy variables MinIO AIStor supports using policy variables for automatically substituting context from the authenticated user and/or the operation into the user’s assigned policy or policies. Use the ${POLICYVARIABLE} format to specify the variable to the policy as part of the Condition or Resource definition. MinIO AIStor policy variables function similarly to AWS IAM policy elements: Variables and tags. MinIO AIStor then evaluates the policy and allows or denies access to the requested resource and action. OpenID policy variables The following table contains a list of supported policy variables for use in authorizing OIDC-managed users. Each variable corresponds to a claim returned as part of the authenticated user’s JWT token: Variable Description jwt:sub Returns the sub claim for the user. jwt:iss Returns the Issuer Identifier claim from the ID token. jwt:aud Returns the Audience claim from the ID token. jwt:jti Returns the JWT ID claim from the client authentication information. jwt:upn Returns the User Principal Name claim from the client authentication information. jwt:name Returns the name claim for the user. jwt:groups Returns the groups claim for the user. jwt:given_name Returns the given_name claim for the user. jwt:family_name Returns the family_name claim for the user. jwt:middle_name Returns the middle_name claim for the user. jwt:nickname Returns the nickname claim for the user. jwt:preferred_username Returns the preferred_username claim for the user. jwt:profile Returns the profile claim for the user. jwt:picture Returns the picture claim for the user. jwt:website Returns the website claim for the user. jwt:email Returns the email claim for the user. jwt:gender Returns the gender claim for the user. jwt:birthdate Returns the birthdate claim for the user. jwt:phone_number Returns the phone_number claim for the user. jwt:address Returns the address claim for the user. jwt:scope Returns the scope claim for the user. jwt:client_id Returns the client_id claim for the user. See the OpenID Connect Core 1.0 specification for more information on these scopes. Your OIDC provider of choice may have more specific documentation. For example, the following policy uses variables to substitute the authenticated user’s preferred_username as part of the Resource field such that the user can only access those prefixes which match their username: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Action": ["s3:ListBucket"], "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::mybucket"], "Condition": {"StringLike": {"s3:prefix": ["${jwt:preferred_username}/*"]}} }, { "Action": [ "s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject" ], "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::mybucket/${jwt:preferred_username}/*"] } ] } MinIO AIStor replaces the ${jwt:preferred_username} variable in the Resource field with the value of the preferred_username in the JWT token. MinIO AIStor then evaluates the policy and grants or revokes access to the requested API and resource. Active Directory / LDAP policy variables The following table contains a list of supported policy variables for use in authorizing AD/LDAP users: Variable Description ldap:username The simple username (name) for the authenticated user.This is distinct from the user’s DistinguishedName or CommonName. ldap:user The Distinguished Name used by the authenticated user. ldap:groups The Group Distinguished Name for the authenticated user. For example, the following policy uses variables to substitute the authenticated user’s name as part of the Resource field such that the user can only access those prefixes which match their name: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Action": ["s3:ListBucket"], "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::mybucket"], "Condition": {"StringLike": {"s3:prefix": ["${ldap:username}/*"]}} }, { "Action": [ "s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject" ], "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::mybucket/${ldap:username}/*"] } ] } MinIO AIStor replaces the ${ldap:username} variable in the Resource field with the value of the authenticated user’s name. MinIO AIStor then evaluates the policy and grants or revokes access to the requested API and resource.

title: Active Directory/LDAP Access Management | HyperVault DocumentationAuthenticating against AD or LDAP
html:
Active Directory/LDAP Access Management

If you integrate HyperVault with Active Directory (AD/LDAP) as your identity provider, you can also manage access with AD/LDAP. HyperVault can map a user’s Distinguished Name or group Distinguished Names (DNs) to existing policies.

See Active Directory/LDAP Identity Management for configuring the integration.

HyperVault supports configuring one or more Active Directory or LDAP (AD/LDAP) services for external management of user identities.

For identities managed by the external AD/LDAP provider, HyperVault uses the user’s Distinguished Name and attempts to map it against an existing policy.

If the AD/LDAP configuration includes the necessary settings to query the user’s AD/LDAP group membership, HyperVault also uses those group Distinguished Names and attempts to map each against an existing policy

By default, HyperVault denies access to all actions or resources not explicitly allowed by a user’s assigned or inherited policies. Users managed by an AD/LDAP provider must specify the necessary policies as part of the user profile data. If no policies match either the user DN or group DNs, HyperVault blocks all access to actions and resources on the deployment.

You configure the AD/LDAP queries HyperVault issues, both to authenticate the user and to retrieve group membership, when you deploy the cluster with Active Directory / LDAP identity management. Create HyperVault policies that match the Distinguished Names those queries can return.

Authentication and authorization flow

The login flow for an application using Active Directory / LDAP credentials is as follows:

  1. Specify the AD/LDAP credentials to the HyperVault Security Token Service (STS) AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentity API endpoint.

  2. HyperVault verifies the provided credentials against the AD/LDAP server.

  3. HyperVault checks for any policy whose name matches the user Distinguished Name (DN) and assigns that policy to the authenticated user.

    If configured to perform group queries, HyperVault also queries for a list of AD/LDAP groups in which the user has membership. HyperVault checks for any policy whose name matches a returned group DN and assigns that policy to the authenticated user.

  4. HyperVault returns temporary credentials in the STS API response in the form of an access key, secret key, and session token. The credentials have permissions matching those policies whose name matches either the authenticated user DN or a group DN.

HyperVault provides an example Go application ldap.go that handles the full login flow.

AD/LDAP users can alternatively create long-lived access keys associated to their AD/LDAP user Distinguished Name with inherited permissions. The parent user can further restrict those privileges while creating the access keys.

You can create an access key by adding it to your IAM user entry in the Console UI.

You can also run the mc idp ldap accesskey commands to manage the access keys. Specify the user Distinguished Name as the username to which to associate the access keys.

Map policies to user DN

The following commands use mc idp ldap policy attach to associate an existing HyperVault policy with an AD/LDAP User DN.

mc idp ldap policy attach myhypervault consoleAdmin\
--user='cn=sisko,cn=users,dc=example,dc=com'

mc idp ldap policy attach myhypervault readwrite,diagnostics\
--user='cn=dax,cn=users,dc=example,dc=com'

  • HyperVault would assign an authenticated user with DN matching cn=sisko,cn=users,dc=example,dc=com the consoleAdmin policy, granting complete access to the HyperVault server.

  • HyperVault would assign an authenticated user with DN matching cn=dax,cn=users,dc=example,dc=com both the readwrite and diagnostics policies, granting general read/write access to the Object Store and access to diagnostic administrative operations.

  • HyperVault would assign no policies to an authenticated user with DN matching cn=quark,cn=users,dc=example,dc=com and deny all access to API operations.

Map policies to group DN

The following commands run mc idp ldap policy attach to associate an existing HyperVault policy with an AD/LDAP Group DN.

mc idp ldap policy attach myhypervault consoleAdmin\
--group='cn=ops,cn=groups,dc=example,dc=com'

mc idp ldap policy attach myhypervault diagnostics\
--group='cn=engineering,cn=groups,dc=example,dc=com'

  • HyperVault would assign any authenticating user with membership in the cn=ops,cn=groups,dc=example,dc=com AD/LDAP group the consoleAdmin policy, granting complete access to the HyperVault server.

  • HyperVault would assign any authenticating user with membership in the cn=engineering,cn=groups,dc=example,dc=com AD/LDAP group the diagnostics policy, granting access to diagnostic administrative operations.

Multiple DN policy mappings

Starting in HyperVault RELEASE.2025-06-20T23-57-47Z, DNs are normalized to be lower case only when loaded. In the case of multiple DNs that normalize to the same value, automatic policies from DNs might not work as expected. You should check to make sure the appropriate policies are applied to your LDAP users. You might see a warning if DN precedence is not clear. To resolve the warning, run mc idp ldap policy attach to specify the desired policy.

title: OpenID Connect Access Management | HyperVault DocumentationAuthenticating against an OIDC provider
html:
OpenID Connect Access Management

For identities managed by an external OpenID Connect (OIDC) compatible provider, HyperVault can use either of two methods to assign policies to the authenticated user.

HyperVault by default denies access to all actions or resources not explicitly allowed by a user’s assigned or inherited policies.

Authorization options with OIDC

OIDC integration in HyperVault supports either of the following authorization methods:

  • The RolePolicy flow sets the assigned policies for an authenticated user in the HyperVault configuration.

    This is the recommended method.

  • The JWT flow sets the assigned policies for an authenticated user as part of the OIDC configuration.

    You can set policies with this method for only one OIDC provider per deployment. If your deployment integrates multiple OIDC providers, all others must set policies with RolePolicy.

  • Users can create long-lived access keys.

    Access keys inherit their permissions from the parent user. The parent user can further restrict permissions when they create access keys. To create a new access key, a human user logs into the Console UI with their OIDC credentials. They can then create an access key in the Access section of the navigation.

RolePolicy and RoleArn

With this flow, a client generates an STS credential with a given RoleArn. The client then receives the policy or policies associated with the RolePolicy configuration for the RoleArn.

You can use OIDC policy variables to create policies that programmatically manage what each individual user has access to.

The flow for an application using OIDC credentials with a RolePolicy claim flow looks like the following:

  1. Create an OIDC Configuration.

  2. Record the RoleArn assigned to the configuration either at time of creation or at HyperVault start. Use this RoleArn with the AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity STS API.

  3. Create a RolePolicy to attach to the RoleArn. Use either the HYPERVAULT_IDENTITY_OPENID_ROLE_POLICY environment variable or the identity_openid role_policy configuration setting to define the list of policies.

  4. Users select the configured OIDC provider when logging in to HyperVault.

  5. Users complete authentication to the configured OIDC provider and redirect back to HyperVault.

    Only the Authorization Code flow is supported. The Implicit flow is not supported.

  6. HyperVault verifies the RoleArn in the API call and checks for the RolePolicy to use. Any authentication request with the RoleArn receives the same policy access permissions.

  7. HyperVault returns temporary credentials in the STS API response in the form of an access key, secret key, and session token. The credentials have permissions matching the policies specified in the RolePolicy.

  8. Applications use the temporary credentials returned by the STS endpoint to perform authenticated S3 operations on HyperVault.

JSON Web Token claim

Using JSON Web Tokens lets you assign policies individually. However, their use comes at the increased cost of managing multiple policies for separate claims.

The login flow for an application using OIDC credentials with a JSON Web Token claim flow looks like the following:

  1. Authenticate to the configured OIDC provider and retrieve a JSON Web Token (JWT).

    Only the Authorization Code flow is supported. The Implicit flow is not supported.

  2. Pass the JWT to the STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity API endpoint.

    HyperVault verifies the JWT against the configured OIDC provider.

    If the JWT is valid, HyperVault checks for a claim specifying a list of one or more policies to assign to the authenticated user. HyperVault defaults to checking the policy claim.

  3. HyperVault returns temporary credentials in the STS API response in the form of an access key, secret key, and session token. The credentials have permissions matching the policies specified in the JWT claim.

  4. Applications use the temporary credentials returned by the STS endpoint to perform authenticated S3 operations on HyperVault.

HyperVault provides an example Go application web-identity.go that handles the full login flow.

Identifying the JWT claim value

HyperVault uses the JWT token returned as part of the OIDC authentication flow to identify the specific policies to assign to the authenticated user.

You can use a JWT Debugging tool to decode the returned JWT token and validate that the user attributes include the required claims.

See RFC 7519: JWT Claim for more information on JWT claims.

Refer to the documentation for your preferred OIDC provider for instructions on configuring user claims.

Microsoft Entra ID group-based authorization

When using Microsoft Entra ID as your OIDC provider with vendor="azure", HyperVault automatically fetches user group memberships from the Microsoft Graph API and populates the azure_groups claim.

HyperVault allows you to manage policies using human-readable Microsoft Entra ID group names instead of UUIDs. When users authenticate, HyperVault assigns all policies that match their Microsoft Entra ID group memberships.

See OpenID Connect Identity Management for Microsoft Entra ID configuration details.

Create policies to match claims

You can use either the Console UI or the mc admin policy command to create policies that match one or more claim values.

OIDC policy variables

The following table contains a list of supported policy variables for use in authorizing OIDC-managed users.

Each variable corresponds to a claim returned as part of the authenticated user’s JWT token:

Variable Description
jwt:sub Returns the sub claim for the user.
jwt:iss Returns the Issuer Identifier claim from the ID token.
jwt:aud Returns the Audience claim from the ID token.
jwt:jti Returns the JWT ID claim from the client authentication information.
jwt:upn Returns the User Principal Name claim from the client authentication information.
jwt:name Returns the name claim for the user.
jwt:groups Returns the groups claim for the user.
jwt:given_name Returns the given_name claim for the user.
jwt:family_name Returns the family_name claim for the user.
jwt:middle_name Returns the middle_name claim for the user.
jwt:nickname Returns the nickname claim for the user.
jwt:preferred_username Returns the preferred_username claim for the user.
jwt:profile Returns the profile claim for the user.
jwt:picture Returns the picture claim for the user.
jwt:website Returns the website claim for the user.
jwt:email Returns the email claim for the user.
jwt:gender Returns the gender claim for the user.
jwt:birthdate Returns the birthdate claim for the user.
jwt:phone_number Returns the phone_number claim for the user.
jwt:address Returns the address claim for the user.
jwt:scope Returns the scope claim for the user.
jwt:client_id Returns the client_id claim for the user.

See the OpenID Connect Core 1.0 document for more information on these scopes. Your OIDC provider of choice may have more specific documentation.

For example, the following policy uses variables to substitute the authenticated user’s preferred_username as part of the Resource field such that the user can access only the prefixes that match their username:

{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
      {
         "Action": ["s3:ListBucket"],
         "Effect": "Allow",
         "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::mybucket"],
         "Condition": {"StringLike": {"s3:prefix": ["${jwt:preferred_username}/*"]}}
      },
      {
         "Action": [
         "s3:GetObject",
         "s3:PutObject"
         ],
         "Effect": "Allow",
         "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::mybucket/${jwt:preferred_username}/*"]
      }
   ]
}

HyperVault replaces the ${jwt:preferred_username} variable in the Resource field with the value of the preferred_username in the JWT token. HyperVault then evaluates the policy and grants or revokes access to the requested actions and resource.

Each variable corresponds to a claim returned as part of the authenticated user’s JWT token: Variable Description jwt:sub Returns the sub claim for the user. jwt:iss Returns the Issuer Identifier claim from the ID token. jwt:aud Returns the Audience claim from the ID token. jwt:jti Returns the JWT ID claim from the client authentication information. jwt:upn Returns the User Principal Name claim from the client authentication information. jwt:name Returns the name claim for the user. jwt:groups Returns the groups claim for the user. jwt:given_name Returns the given_name claim for the user. jwt:family_name Returns the family_name claim for the user. jwt:middle_name Returns the middle_name claim for the user. jwt:nickname Returns the nickname claim for the user. jwt:preferred_username Returns the preferred_username claim for the user. jwt:profile Returns the profile claim for the user. jwt:picture Returns the picture claim for the user. jwt:website Returns the website claim for the user. jwt:email Returns the email claim for the user. jwt:gender Returns the gender claim for the user. jwt:birthdate Returns the birthdate claim for the user. jwt:phone_number Returns the phone_number claim for the user. jwt:address Returns the address claim for the user. jwt:scope Returns the scope claim for the user. jwt:client_id Returns the client_id claim for the user. See the OpenID Connect Core 1.0 document for more information on these scopes. Your OIDC provider of choice may have more specific documentation. For example, the following policy uses variables to substitute the authenticated user’s preferred_username as part of the Resource field such that the user can access only the prefixes that match their username: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Action": ["s3:ListBucket"], "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::mybucket"], "Condition": {"StringLike": {"s3:prefix": ["${jwt:preferred_username}/*"]}} }, { "Action": [ "s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject" ], "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::mybucket/${jwt:preferred_username}/*"] } ] } MinIO AIStor replaces the ${jwt:preferred_username} variable in the Resource field with the value of the preferred_username in the JWT token. MinIO AIStor then evaluates the policy and grants or revokes access to the requested actions and resource.

title: Authorization Plugin | HyperVault DocumentationAuthorizing through a webhook
html:
Authorization Plugin

The HyperVault Access Management Plugin provides a REST interface for offloading authorization through a webhook service.

HyperVault sends the request and credential details for every API call to the configured external HTTP(S) endpoint and looks for a response of ALLOW or DENY. HyperVault can therefore delegate the access management to the external system instead of relying on S3 policy based access control.

Open Policy Agent is a common choice for the endpoint. It works with any credential type: OpenID or LDAP STS credentials, built-in users, and access keys alike.

The endpoint receives every request header, so use HTTPS

The request body carries the whole conditions map, which includes every header the client sent. That means the Authorization header, X-Amz-Security-Token, and on SSE-C requests the object encryption key in X-Amz-Server-Side-Encryption-Customer-Key. Your HYPERVAULT_POLICY_PLUGIN_AUTH_TOKEN travels as an Authorization header on the same request.

HyperVault accepts both http:// and https:// and does not warn you about a plaintext endpoint. Use HTTPS for any endpoint that is not on the loopback interface.

What the endpoint decides, and what it does not

When the plugin is configured, HyperVault consults it before anything else, so the endpoint answers for every authenticated identity. That includes the root user, whose usual bypass is not reached. An endpoint that does not explicitly allow the owner locks the root user out of the deployment, so grant it deliberately.

If the endpoint cannot be reached, or answers with anything HyperVault cannot parse, the request is denied. The decision is not cached, so the endpoint’s availability and latency become the deployment’s availability and latency for authorization.

Two paths still decide on their own and never reach the endpoint:

  • Anonymous requests, which carry no credentials, are decided by the bucket policy.
  • Internal HyperVault Tables access is refused before authorization runs.

If your credentials carry an inline session policy, the endpoint has to apply it. HyperVault does not evaluate the session policy separately once the plugin is in the path.

Every authenticated request calls the endpoint
This is not a login-time check. Each authenticated API call triggers one request to the plugin, so the endpoint sits in the latency path of every operation. Size and place it accordingly, and measure before putting it in front of a latency-sensitive workload.

Configuration settings

You can configure the HyperVault External Access Management Plugin using the following environment variables or configuration settings.

Specify the following environmental variables for each object store in the deployment:

HYPERVAULT_POLICY_PLUGIN_URL="https://external-authz.example.net:8080/authz"

# All other envvars are optional
HYPERVAULT_POLICY_PLUGIN_AUTH_TOKEN="Bearer TOKEN"
HYPERVAULT_POLICY_PLUGIN_ENABLE_HTTP2="OFF"
HYPERVAULT_POLICY_PLUGIN_COMMENT="External Access Management using PROVIDER"

Specify the following configuration settings with the mc admin config set command:

mc admin config set policy_plugin \
   url="https://external-authz.example.net:8080/authz" \

   # All other config settings are optional
   auth_token="Bearer TOKEN" \
   enable_http2="off" \
   comment="External Access Management using PROVIDER"

Authentication and authorization flow

The login flow for an application is as follows:

  1. The client includes authentication information as part of performing the API call

  2. The configured Identity Manager authenticates the client

  3. HyperVault makes a POST call to the configured access management plugin URL which includes the context of the API call and authentication data

  4. On successful authorization, the access manager returns a 200 OK response with a JSON body of either result true or "result" : { "allow" : true }:

If the access manager rejects the authorization request, HyperVault automatically blocks and denies the API call.

Request body example

The following JSON resembles the request body sent as part of the POST to the configured access manager webhook.

{
   "input": {
      "account": "hypervault",
      "groups": null,
      "action": "s3:ListBucket",
      "bucket": "test",
      "conditions": {
         "Authorization": [
         "AWS4-HMAC-SHA256 Credential=hypervault/20220507/us-east-1/s3/aws4_request, SignedHeaders=host;x-amz-content-sha256;x-amz-date, Signature=62012db6c47d697620cf6c68f0f45f6e34894589a53ab1faf6dc94338468c78a"
         ],
         "CurrentTime": [ "2022-05-07T18:31:41Z" ],
         "Delimiter": [ "/" ],
         "EpochTime": [
         "1651948301"
         ],
         "Prefix": [ "" ],
         "Referer": [ "" ],
         "SecureTransport": [ "false" ],
         "SourceIp": [ "127.0.0.1" ],
         "User-Agent": [ "HyperVault (linux; amd64) hypervault-go/v7.0.24 mc/DEVELOPMENT.2022-04-20T23-07-53Z" ],
         "UserAgent": [ "HyperVault (linux; amd64) hypervault-go/v7.0.24 mc/DEVELOPMENT.2022-04-20T23-07-53Z" ],
         "X-Amz-Content-Sha256": [ "e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855" ],
         "X-Amz-Date": [ "20220507T183141Z" ],
         "authType": [ "REST-HEADER" ],
         "principaltype": [ "Account" ],
         "signatureversion": [ "AWS4-HMAC-SHA256" ],
         "userid": [ "hypervault" ],
         "username": [ "hypervault" ],
         "versionid": [ "" ]
      },
      "owner": true,
      "object": "",
      "claims": {},
      "denyOnly": false
   }
}

Response body example

HyperVault requires the response body from the Access Management service meet one of the two following formats:

{ "result" : true }

{ "result" : { "allow" : true } }

title: HyperVault Identity Management | HyperVault Documentation
html:
HyperVault Identity Management

HyperVault supports multiple identity providers for authenticating users and applications. You can use the built-in identity management system, integrate with external identity providers, or combine multiple providers to support different groups of users.

See Identity and Access Management for an overview of how identity and access control work together in HyperVault.

Identity providers

HyperVault supports the following identity providers:

Provider Description
Built-in Manage users and groups directly within HyperVault using access key and secret key credentials.
OpenID Connect (OIDC) Integrate with OIDC-compatible identity providers such as Okta, Auth0, Keycloak, or Google.
Active Directory/LDAP Authenticate users against Active Directory or LDAP directory services.
X.509 certificate Authenticate with a client certificate or a SPIFFE SVID, with no external provider in the request path.
Kubernetes service account Authenticate in-cluster workloads with the service account token Kubernetes already gives them.
Authentication plugin Implement custom authentication logic with an external identity management plugin.

Multiple identity providers

HyperVault supports configuring multiple identity providers simultaneously. You can implement built-in user management together with one or more external identity providers to support different user groups or authentication requirements.

HyperVault supports using any combination of the following providers:

Provider Type Multiple Allowed Notes
Built-in users N/A Always available for direct S3 access
AD/LDAP Yes Each with a unique configuration name
OpenID (role-based) Yes Each with a unique Role ARN
OpenID (claim-based) One only Can combine with role-based providers
Authentication plugins Yes External authentication services

Vendor guides for OpenID Connect

Three providers have their own walkthrough on top of the general OIDC configuration: Keycloak, Microsoft Entra ID, formerly Azure AD, and Okta.

title: Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) Identity Provider | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) Identity Provider

Configure Microsoft Entra ID, formerly Azure Active Directory, as an OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider for HyperVault. For general OIDC configuration, see OpenID Connect Identity Management.

Prerequisites

  • An active Azure subscription with access to the Azure Portal.
  • A HyperVault deployment with network connectivity to Microsoft identity endpoints.
  • The mc CLI installed and configured with an alias for your HyperVault deployment.

Microsoft Graph API permissions

HyperVault uses the Microsoft Graph API to query group memberships for authenticated users. The following Application permissions are required (not Delegated):

Permission Purpose
User.Read.All Read user profiles and group memberships
Group.Read.All Read group information and memberships

These permissions require admin consent and enable HyperVault to:

  • Query the /users/{user-id}/memberGroups endpoint
  • Map Azure AD security groups and Microsoft 365 groups to HyperVault policies

Register an application in Azure

  1. In the Azure Portal, navigate to Microsoft Entra ID > App registrations > New registration.
  2. Enter a name (for example, hypervault-oidc).
  3. Set Supported account types as appropriate for your organization.
  4. Set Redirect URI platform to Web and enter your Console UI URL: 
    https://hypervault.example.com/oauth_callback
  5. Select Register.

After registration:

  1. Note the Application (client) ID and Directory (tenant) ID.
  2. Navigate to Certificates & secrets > New client secret. Copy the generated secret value for HYPERVAULT_IDENTITY_OPENID_CLIENT_SECRET.
  3. Navigate to API permissions > Add a permission > Microsoft Graph > Application permissions. Add User.Read.All and Group.Read.All.
  4. Select Grant admin consent for your organization.

The OpenID discovery document URL is:

https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration

Configure HyperVault

Add the Azure AD provider using mc:

mc idp openid add ALIAS azure \
  config_url="https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration" \
  client_id="<client-id>" \
  client_secret="<client-secret>" \
  scopes="openid,email,profile" \
  redirect_uri="https://hypervault.example.com/oauth_callback" \
  display_name="Azure AD" \
  claim_name="azure_groups" \
  vendor="azure" \
  azure_tenant_id="<tenant-id>"

Or using environment variables:

export HYPERVAULT_IDENTITY_OPENID_CONFIG_URL="https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration"
export HYPERVAULT_IDENTITY_OPENID_CLIENT_ID="<client-id>"
export HYPERVAULT_IDENTITY_OPENID_CLIENT_SECRET="<client-secret>"
export HYPERVAULT_IDENTITY_OPENID_SCOPES="openid,email,profile"
export HYPERVAULT_IDENTITY_OPENID_REDIRECT_URI="https://hypervault.example.com/oauth_callback"
export HYPERVAULT_IDENTITY_OPENID_DISPLAY_NAME="Azure AD"
export HYPERVAULT_IDENTITY_OPENID_CLAIM_NAME="azure_groups"
export HYPERVAULT_IDENTITY_OPENID_VENDOR="azure"
export HYPERVAULT_IDENTITY_OPENID_AZURE_TENANT_ID="<tenant-id>"

Restart HyperVault to apply the configuration:

mc admin service restart ALIAS

Azure-specific settings

Setting Value Purpose
vendor azure Enables Microsoft Graph API integration for group membership
azure_tenant_id your tenant ID Required for client credentials authentication to Graph API
claim_name azure_groups Maps Azure AD group claims to HyperVault policies

How group mapping works

  1. A user authenticates via Azure AD OIDC and HyperVault receives an access token.
  2. HyperVault calls the userinfo endpoint to get the user’s object ID (oid claim).
  3. HyperVault authenticates to the Microsoft Graph API using the configured tenant ID, client ID, and client secret.
  4. HyperVault queries the Graph API to retrieve all security groups the user belongs to.
  5. These groups are added to the azure_groups claim for policy mapping.

Periodic group refresh

To keep group memberships current, add offline_access to the scopes configuration:

mc idp openid update ALIAS azure scopes="openid,email,profile,offline_access"

This enables HyperVault to periodically refresh group information from Azure AD (approximately once per hour).

Log in with Azure AD

  1. Open the Console UI in a browser.
  2. Select Login with SSO.
  3. Enter your Azure AD credentials on the Microsoft login page.
  4. After successful authentication, you are redirected to the Console UI with access based on your Azure AD group policies.
